title: Trump's Approval Just Hit 35%. Indian Markets Are Watching the Midterms More Closely Than Most Americans.
excerpt: With foreign investors pulling ₹2.2 lakh crore out of Indian equities this year and the rupee under pressure, Dalal Street is betting that a Democratic midterm surge could reshape the trade landscape.
body:
A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on May 19 found Donald Trump's overall approval rating at 35 per cent — the lowest of his second term. His approval on cost-of-living issues has cratered to just 22 per cent. Nearly two-thirds of voters said the president made the wrong decision in going to war with Iran. Even his Republican base is showing cracks.

Six months before American voters head to the polls for the 2026 midterm elections, these numbers are being parsed as carefully on Dalal Street as they are on Capitol Hill — and for reasons that have everything to do with money flowing out of Mumbai and into Washington's policy machinery.

## The Great Exodus

Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn a staggering ₹2.2 lakh crore from Indian equities so far in 2026, already exceeding the ₹1.66 lakh crore pulled out during the entirety of 2025. In May alone, FPIs have sold ₹27,048 crore worth of shares. The Sensex has shed more than 8 per cent year-to-date; the Nifty 50 has fallen over 5 per cent.

The causes are layered: elevated crude oil prices driven by the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, a strong dollar siphoning capital back to American treasuries, high bond yields, and — crucially — the punitive 25 per cent tariff that Trump slapped on India last year for purchasing discounted Russian oil. That single policy decision forced New Delhi to scramble for alternative energy suppliers and sent a chill through export-dependent sectors.

India's macroeconomic fundamentals remain robust — GDP growth of 7.4-7.8 per cent, inflation cooling to 3.48 per cent in April, and the Reserve Bank of India holding the repo rate steady at 5.25 per cent. But fundamentals have been no match for the geopolitical headwinds emanating from Washington.

## Why the Midterms Matter

Here is the calculation that fund managers in both Mumbai and New York are making: if Trump's approval continues to erode, a strong Democratic performance in the November 2026 midterms could strip Republicans of their congressional majorities. That, in turn, could constrain the administration's ability to impose further tariffs, escalate foreign conflicts, or pursue the kind of unpredictable economic brinksmanship that has spooked global capital markets.

"Markets are forward-looking instruments," said one Mumbai-based portfolio strategist. "The moment there's a credible signal that the tariff regime might soften or that there will be institutional checks on Iran policy, you'll see capital rotate back into emerging markets — India first among them."

The logic has historical precedent. After the 2018 midterms, when Democrats took the House, the S&P 500 rallied and emerging-market equities stabilised as investors priced in divided government constraining trade-war escalation.

## The NRI Investor's Dilemma

For the estimated 18 million members of the Indian diaspora, many of whom maintain investment portfolios in both countries, the current moment presents a peculiar dilemma. American retirement accounts have benefited from a strong dollar and resilient Wall Street performance. But Indian holdings — mutual funds, direct equity, real estate — have been battered by the very policies that are propping up the dollar.

Remittances, too, are caught in the crossfire. The rupee has weakened to record lows against the dollar, which means that every dollar sent home buys more rupees — a boon for families in India, but a reflection of underlying economic stress that no one finds reassuring.

NRI investors who rebalanced toward Indian equities during the 2024 rally are now sitting on paper losses. Those who held cash in dollar accounts have been inadvertently rewarded. The divergence is widening, and the political outcome of the midterms may well determine which side of the trade proves wise.

## The Bigger Picture

India's market regulators are watching closely. SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey recently insisted that Indian markets are "resilient to West Asia shocks," but the data tells a more complicated story. The reality is that India, for all its domestic growth, remains deeply integrated into global capital flows — and those flows are, at this moment, being shaped more by the political fortunes of one American president than by any earnings season or monetary policy decision in Mumbai.

The midterms are still six months away. A great deal can change. But the unusual spectacle of Indian traders refreshing American polling data alongside their Bloomberg terminals is itself a marker of how interconnected — and how fragile — the global financial architecture has become. For the diaspora straddling both worlds, November cannot come soon enough.
